consensus_summary: The consensus identifies righteousness broadly as rightness according to God, centrally including right standing before God granted by grace and also moral conformity, just conduct, or transformed living.
book_summary: The book identifies righteousness principally with actual right-living: God’s own right ways and, for those under him, obedience to his commandments. Grace gives and reckons righteousness but does not classify wrong conduct as righteous.
consensus_core_identification: A right status or relationship before God, together with or resulting in conformity to God’s character and will.
book_core_identification: Actual right-living measured by God’s ways and expressed in doing his commandments.
boundary_disagreement: Both include obedient and morally right conduct, but the consensus permits righteousness to denote a gracious forensic or relational standing distinct from subsequent conduct. The book reclassifies such standing: righteousness itself is right-living, even when graciously given or reckoned, and wrong-living is never made righteous by declaration.
material_contradiction: The mainstream identification makes right standing the central referent and commonly treats right-living as its fruit or evidence; the book makes right-living the referent itself. Thus it replaces a status-centered identification with a conduct-centered one, although that conduct-centered sense is represented among the consensus alternatives.
rationale: This is not novel because ethical, transformative, and command-conforming senses appear throughout the consensus. It is nevertheless divergent from the consensus’s central status-plus-conformity identification because the book denies the usual distinction between righteousness as standing and righteous living as its product. Their extensions overlap in genuinely obedient lives, but they classify a person declared righteous apart from present works differently.
strongest_objection: Romans 4:5–8 explicitly speaks of God justifying the ungodly and imputing righteousness without works, while Philippians 3:9 contrasts righteousness from the law with righteousness through faith. These texts can naturally support righteousness as a granted status distinct from actual command-keeping, so the printed citations do not by themselves establish the book’s restrictive claim that righteousness denotes right-living rather than standing.
